analysis.one_liner: Lets states open Medicaid to any resident who buys in, with premiums capped at 8.5% of income.
analysis.headline: A Democratic bill to let states offer a Medicaid buy-in to any resident never got a hearing, markup, or vote; it sat in two House committees from March 2024 until the Congress ended in January 2025, with 9 Democratic cosponsors and none from the other party.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let each state choose to open its Medicaid program to any resident who is not already covered, letting them buy in with premiums capped at 8.5% of family income and with the same federal tax credits that subsidize marketplace insurance plans. It would also give a permanent federal bonus to states that expand Medicaid late, require state Medicaid programs to cover sexual and reproductive health care including abortion, and guarantee primary care doctors and clinics Medicare-level payment rates for treating Medicaid patients. It never received any committee hearing or floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured and underinsured residents of states that opt in, people stuck without affordable coverage in states that never expanded Medicaid, patients who need reproductive health care, and primary care providers who would be paid Medicare rates for Medicaid patients.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured residents and primary care providers

how_it_helps.text: Any state could open Medicaid to residents not eligible for it now, letting them buy in at premiums capped at 8.5% of family income with cost-sharing limited to the rules that apply to marketplace plans.

Buy-in enrollees would qualify for the same premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions as people buying marketplace plans, with the state Medicaid agency treated like an exchange for subsidy purposes.
States that expand Medicaid at any point would get the enhanced federal match on the same schedule as states that expanded in 2014, removing the penalty for waiting.

Medicaid would have to pay primary care providers at least Medicare rates, a rule revived and expanded to obstetricians, nurse practitioners, physician assistants, certified nurse-midwives, and community health clinics, and managed care plans would have to pass those rates through.
State Medicaid programs would be required to cover comprehensive sexual and reproductive health care, including abortion services, as a condition of federal plan approval.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the 90% administrative match, higher expansion matches, and premium tax credits; states cover their share of costs; private insurers lose potential customers to a cheaper public plan.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal and state governments, private insurers

drawbacks.text: Each state decides whether to participate, so people in states that opt out would get nothing; the help is uneven by geography.
Families could still owe premiums up to a full 8.5% of household income, a real cost for households already stretched thin.

The bill would route the new coverage through Medicaid's existing structure, including private managed care plans, so much of the spending would still flow through insurance intermediaries rather than directly to doctors and patients.

The mandate that state Medicaid programs cover abortion goes far beyond current federal policy, which restricts most federal Medicaid funding for abortion, and would make the bill a flashpoint that states and opponents would contest.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: a cheaper public insurance option for people the private market hasn't served well, paid for by federal subsidies and by private insurers' lost sales. The main weaknesses are that it is voluntary for states, so its reach depends on where you live, and that premiums of up to 8.5% of income can still be unaffordable for many. The primary-care payment floor is a genuine add for access in Medicaid, where low payment rates keep many doctors from participating. On balance it is a real, though geographically uneven, expansion of affordable coverage.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees and to their health subcommittees, and neither panel ever scheduled a hearing or markup before the Congress ended, so there was never a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Kim Schrier introduced the bill on March 22, 2024, joined by nine Democratic colleagues.
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee the same day.
It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee in March 2024 and again in December 2024, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died without any committee or floor action beyond referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private insurers keep the individual market without a lower-cost public competitor, and the status quo holds for the states that never expanded Medicaid, their residents, and the primary care practices that continue to be paid low Medicaid rates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers and the status quo

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled committees that held the bill took no action on it.

industries.note: A Medicaid buy-in, subsidized with the same tax credits as marketplace plans, would give consumers a lower-cost public alternative to commercial exchange plans, reducing insurers' enrollment and leverage over premiums. Insurers had an interest in keeping this bill off the floor.

The bill extends Medicaid managed care rules to buy-in enrollees, so states could route the new public coverage through private managed care plans, giving them enrollment; but the same contracts would have to pay primary care providers at Medicare-level rates, squeezing what insurers keep.

industries.industry: Primary care providers (physicians, clinics, nurse practitioners)
industries.note: The bill revives and expands a rule requiring Medicaid to pay primary care at Medicare rates and requires managed care plans to pass those rates through, directly raising what these providers earn for serving Medicaid patients.
